title: Researchers reveal inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi using multisensor satellite observations

DOI: 10.34133/remotesensing.1095 Tropical cyclones frequently undergo rapid, complex structural changes within their inner cores, such as eyewall replacement and wind-field expansion, that strongly influence typhoon intensity and coastal hazards. However, capturing these multilayered transformations continuously from the ocean surface to the upper cloud tops remains a major observational challenge. To address this challenge, a research team from the Institute of Oceanology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (IOCAS) reconstructed the full inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi by integrating 17 repeated spaceborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) overpasses with geostationary infrared imagery and synthetic microwave brightness temperature fields. Their findings were published in the Journal of Remote Sensing on Nov. 11. Tracking the typhoon across vertical layers To track the typhoon across multiple vertical levels simultaneously, the researchers combined near-surface ocean wind fields derived from NOAA/STAR tropical cyclone SAR products with cloud-top center positions identified from the Japan Meteorological Agency's Himawari-9 infrared observations. In addition, they generated hourly synthetic 89-GHz microwave brightness temperature fields from multispectral infrared measurements to monitor deep convection and eyewall reorganization around the typhoon's eye. These integrated satellite observations uncovered a clear temporal sequence in how the typhoon's inner core reorganized: A secondary eyewall formed and contracted inward first, followed by a pronounced horizontal separation between the near-surface circulation center and the upper-level cloud-top center. Finally, the typhoon's strong-wind region expanded substantially during its weakening stage. "Coordinated multisensor observations provide a rare vertical cross section of a typhoon's life cycle," said Dr. Mu Shanshan, first author of the study. By pairing repeated high-resolution SAR wind snapshots with continuous geostationary infrared and synthetic microwave tracking, the researchers can pinpoint the exact timing of eyewall replacement, vertical vortex tilt and near-surface wind broadening. Eyewall replacement precedes growing vortex tilt Between 00:00 UTC on July 5 and July 6, the synthetic 89-GHz imagery captured the formation, intensification and inward contraction of the outer eyewall, showing that the eyewall replacement cycle concluded around 23:00 UTC on July 6. During the initial formation of the secondary eyewall, the horizontal offset between the near-surface circulation center and the infrared cloud-top center (defined as the SAR–IR tilt) was relatively small at roughly 5 to 10 km (3 to 6 miles). As the replacement process neared completion, this offset widened to 17.8 km (11.1 miles) and further increased to 20.8 km (12.9 miles) in observations on July 7. Weaker winds spread over a wider area High-resolution SAR wind retrievals further revealed that as Typhoon Bavi weakened in its later stages, its maximum near-surface wind speed declined overall while its radius of maximum wind (RMW) expanded dramatically. During the typhoon's peak intensity phase, the RMW was tightly concentrated between 15 and 26 km (9 and 16 miles).
